newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - Chart trade, 5-yr sale.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - Chart trade, 5-yr sale.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury market will ease into trade Wednesday focusing on the government's five-year note sale and chart-driven activity given an absence until next week of key economic data, market experts said.

"(Tuesday's) two-year auction was ok; actually, it turned out better than most people expected," said Cary Leahey, senior financial market economist at Lehman Government Securities Inc. "But when you have a two-year that goes better than expected, you usually get a five-year that goes worse than expected."

Treasury will sell $12.5 billion in five-year notes at its regular monthly auction on Wednesday. The sale follows a $17.009 billion auction of two-year notes on Tuesday. The two-year paper fetched a yield of 6.46 percent.
With only the five-year note auction and appearances by two Federal Reserve Bank presidents, economists and dealers said technical factors would dominate Wednesday's trade.

"The market is headed lower in terms of price," said David Ging, technical market analyst at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp, adding he was not surprised by the long bond's recent bounce off a cushion of support at 7.07 percent.

"But that rebound is starting to run out of steam," he said. "The seasonal factors through the middle and end of May point down. So it's looks like we're going to trade lower into the next (Fed policy) meeting."

Ging said he examined average Treasury price movements from mid-April to mid- to late-May over the past 11 years, and noticed that these so-called "seasonal factors" show a strong tendency for the market to trade lower during that period.
He said these tendencies were prevalent in each individual year as well as in averages for the 11-year period.

Meanwhile, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), the central bank's policy-making arm, next meets on May 20. Central bankers are widely expected to hike short-term interest rates again by 25 basis points at that time.
Ging said traders were eyeing 7.25 percent for the 30-year yield near term, adding that he expected the quarter-point mark to be tackled "over the next week or two."
Beyond that, Ging said 7.31 percent represented a 61.8 percent retracement target from the 1994 yield high to the 1996 yield low. "And then there's 7.50 after that," he said.

Separately, the Chicago Federal Reserve Bank will hold a symposium entitled "Assessing the Midwest Economy: Looking Back for the Future," in Chicago. The event will start at 0930 EDT/1330 GMT on Wednesday, and speakers include Chicago Fed President Michael Moskow, Illinois Governor Jim Edgar, and several senior economists from the Chicago Fed.
In addition, Atlanta Federal Reserve Bank President Jack Guynn will discuss the U.S. economic outlook and the future of banking at two events in Murfreesboro, Tenn.

Guynn will address the local Chamber of Commerce and then speak to students, faculty, and members of the community at Middle Tennessee State University. Guynn's first appearance is scheduled to begin at 1255 EDT/1655 GMT and the second at 1430 EDT/1830 GMT.

"You always have the possibility for 'tape bombs," Leahey said in a reference to comments by Fed and other officials that appear on newswire feeds. "But other than those tape bombs, there's really no data to chew on."
The benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond closed up about 20/32 on Tuesday at 94-28/32 to yield 7.04 percent.
